title: optimize-console-api-aggregation-executor-prefetch-and-dependency-bump
creator: Aisha Kumar
description:
Summary: Reduce end-to-end tail latency and CPU contention in the Console backend aggregation path by decoupling the aggregation executor, introducing a small prefetch layer for dashboard queries, and sharding cache keys to reduce cache hot spots. This ticket also includes a controlled dependency upgrade (GraphQL server, Redis client, Node LTS) needed for the new executor and connection pooling improvements.

Background: Over the last 6 months we've seen intermittent tail latency spikes and elevated CPU usage on the console aggregation service during large org dashboard loads. Root causes include: single-threaded aggregation executor doing heavy merge logic synchronously, cache key collisions for frequently requested rollups, and an older Redis client lacking pooled connection reuse semantics. Previous tactical fixes reduced noise but did not address fundamental coupling between request handling and aggregation execution.

Goals:
- Move heavy aggregation work off the API request handler into a bounded executor (worker pool) to reduce per-request CPU jitter.
- Implement a small prefetch layer for common dashboard query prefixes to warm cache/KV and reduce cold-path work for interactive users.
- Shard caching namespace by route+timebucket to avoid cross-route hot keys and enable TTL segmentation.
- Bump graphql-server to 15.9.x and redis client to 5.2.x (or newer recommended stable) to get connection pooling and streaming improvements.
- Expose a feature flag to toggle executor/prefetch behavior for safe canary and rollback.

Scope:
Included: executor implementation, prefetch strategy, cache key sharding, dependency upgrades, metrics & dashboards, rollout plan and runbook.
Excluded: frontend console UI changes, DB schema changes, or wholesale redesign of aggregation algorithms (this is a targeted cleanup).

Implementation notes / approach:
- Introduce aggregation-executor module that accepts lightweight tasks representing merge operations. The HTTP handler will enqueue tasks and await a bounded future with a short timeout; on timeout we fall back to the legacy sync path.
- Prefetcher: route-level configurable list of high-frequency query prefixes. Background worker will run prefetches at low QPS and populate both runtime in-memory prefix cache (small LRU) and Redis with sharded keys.
- Cache sharding: key format -> "aggr::{route}::{timebucket}:{shard_id}::{fingerprint}". Shard_id computed with hashed route+org modulo N (N adjustable per route).
- Dependencies: run CI matrix for node LTS upgrade (16->18 or 18->20 depending on infra), graphql-server upgrade to pick up resolver batching improvements, redis client bump to get pooled connections & auto-retry.
- Feature flagging: rollout via Config Service flags (console.feature.aggregation_executor_v2). Default off for all orgs.

Acceptance criteria:
- 95th percentile API latency for dashboard aggregate endpoints reduced by >=30% in canary orgs compared to baseline.
- P99 latency reduced and tail jitter reduced (qualitative).
- No increase in 5xx error rate for monitored endpoints during canary.
- CPU per pod 95th percentile reduced by at least 15% under representative load tests.
- Automated rollout/rollback via feature flag succeeds in <5 minutes.

Rollout plan:
1) Merge behind feature flag, enable for internal org only. Run load tests and synthetic traffic for 48 hours.
2) Canary: enable for 5 small non-critical orgs for 24 hours. Monitor dashboards and error budget.
3) Gradual ramp to 25% of orgs over 24 hours, then 100% if metrics stable.
4) If any threshold breach, flip feature flag off and failover to legacy path.

Metrics to monitor:
- dashboard.aggregate.api.latency.p50/p95/p99 (by org & route)
- aggregation_executor.queue_depth and task_wait_time (histogram)
- pod_cpu_usage.p95 and pod_memory_usage.p95
- cache_hit_rate (route-specific), redis_command_latency
- 5xx error rate and request timeout counts

Risks & mitigations:
- Risk: Executor queue can become a contention bottleneck under bursty loads. Mitigation: bounded queue + backpressure -> fall back to legacy sync path and log for later investigation.
- Risk: Prefetching could increase load/redis traffic. Mitigation: very conservative QPS cap per route and adaptive backoff if redis latency climbs.
- Risk: Dependency upgrades introduce subtle breaking changes. Mitigation: CI matrix + smoke sandbox + staged canary.

Open questions:
- Target Node LTS version: 18 vs 20 (infra capacity & native lib compatibility).
- Optimal shard count per route (start with 8, tune from telemetry).
- Prefetch key selection: static list maintained in repo vs dynamic top-N sampling.

Artifacts / links:
- Design doc (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Console+Aggregation+Executor+Design
- Prototype PR (prefetch + executor PoC): https://github.com/redwood-inference/console/pull/2834
- Dependency bump PR (node & graphql): https://github.com/redwood-inference/console/pull/2879
- Load test dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/console-agg/load-tests

Notes: keep change small, observable, and reversible. The aim is to reduce operational surprises rather than fully rearchitecting aggregation logic.
acceptance_criteria: 95th percentile dashboard aggregate latency reduced >=30% in canary orgs; p99 latency and CPU p95 reduced; no increase in 5xx; successful feature-flag rollback tested
rollout_plan: internal canary -> 5 small orgs -> 25% -> 100% with feature-flag rollback and 48h synthetic validation windows
risks: executor queue contention (fallback to legacy), prefetch traffic increase (QPS cap & backoff), dependency upgrade regressions (CI matrix & sandbox)
